Closing Dewey and Lincolnwood: what it saves, what it costs

District 65 has proposed closing Dewey and Lincolnwood elementary schools as part of its plan to balance the budget. This page breaks down what the district's published documents show about the savings and the costs, in plain terms, for anyone in the community who wants to understand the proposal. Each figure links to its source.

The short version

86%

Most of the plan doesn't involve closing a school.

$18.5M of the $21.4M plan is on other lines. That alone reaches 92% of the $20M goal. [1] [10]

Closing the two schools likely saves less than the $2.9M claimed.

The $2.9M is gross. The net depends on whether jobs are actually cut and the buildings sold. Last year's closures saved close to nothing in staff. [1] [5]

103

The district files 103 job cuts under "closures and consolidation" without splitting them.

Closing the two schools directly removes about 14 building jobs and 6 to 8 teachers, if the cuts happen. The district doesn't say how many of the 103 come from closing versus combining roles elsewhere. [9] [1] [13]

The target itself isn't explained.

The district ties it to balanced budgets and rebuilding cash reserves to 90 days, but doesn't show how $20M was derived. Without action it projects shortfalls of $3.9M in FY28 rising to $21.6M in FY30. The plan nets $14.9M. [24] [9]

Families carry costs that aren't in the $2.9M.

That many children change schools, by the district's count. Busing and moving costs aren't in the savings figure. [9] [10]

Are the closures needed to balance the budget?

86% of the plan isn't on the closure line. The closures are $2.9M of a $21.4M plan. Without them, the plan comes about $1.5M short of the district's $20M goal, a gap other choices could also fill. [1] [10]

  • The district's October 7 plan lists $21.4M in gross savings and new revenue. Dewey and Lincolnwood are one line: $2.9M, about 14%. [1]
  • Without that line the plan totals $18.5M, about $1.5M short of the district's $20M goal. That gap is about 18 positions at the district's own pricing, or under 1% of yearly operating spending (see below for other ways to reach it). [1] [4] [10]
  • The closures themselves likely deliver less than $2.9M: about $0.1M to $1.8M a year by our estimate (next section). At best they cover it; if staffing goes like last year, they cover almost none of it. [1] [5]
  • The district ties the $20M goal to balanced budgets and rebuilding cash reserves to 90 days, but hasn't shown how it was derived, so it isn't possible to say whether $18.5M would be enough. The plan's largest line, staffing, has its own open questions (below). [1] [10] [9]

FY28 plan by category, gross, as the district states it. [1] The hatched part of the closure line is what our review finds would actually be saved if positions are cut.

The staffing line: 103 positions under "closures and consolidation"

  • The $11.3M staffing line cuts 56 certified, 40 classified and 6 administrative positions ($7.3M) in the October 7 plan. The October 13 presentation lists the same group as 56, 41 and 6, or 103, under the heading "School Closures/Staffing Consolidation." The other $4.0M is healthcare redesign, retirement, overtime and special education changes. [1] [9]
  • Positions, not people. The district can't say which people will be cut: under state law and the teachers' contract, layoffs follow performance ratings and then seniority across the whole district, so a teacher at a closing school may keep a job while someone elsewhere is laid off. Notices go out by April 15. [26] But it can say how many positions in each role come from closing two buildings and how many from consolidating elsewhere, and neither document does. Its pledge that no school-based role is fully eliminated is a choice to spread cuts across roles, not a seniority rule. [9] [1]
  • Closing a school saves fewer classroom teachers than you might expect. Its students spread out across several schools, and a teacher is saved only if they fit into open seats there. When they don't fit, the receiving school has to open a new class. [13] [7] [20]

24 is the district's usual practice, not a hard limit; the teachers' contract sets goals of 23 in K–2 and 25 in grades 3–5. Lincoln's and Foster's 4th grades would reach about 27 in two classes, so the district could keep them at two with extra support instead of opening a class. [26] Dewey's split across the four schools is our estimate; the district hasn't published it. Foster's and Washington's counts leave out their dual-language classes. Orrington is drawn with 3 classes for 52 students, the district's usual rule; its class list currently shows this grade in 2 classes of 26, one of only two grades that break the rule. [13] [7] [20]

See every grade, and where each number comes from

Each square is one class, capped at 24. Next year's grades 1–5 are this fall's K–4. Where the numbers come from. Official D65: this fall's enrollment by school and grade, Lincolnwood's split (269 to Willard, 39 to Walker, 23 STEP to Orrington), each receiving school's projected enrollment, and the rule that all dual-language students go to Lincoln. Our estimates: the district hasn't published Dewey's split, so we derive it. By where they live, Dewey's 314 students would go about 101 to Lincoln, 94 to Foster, 78 to Washington and 41 to Orrington. Foster 94 is the district's Foster projection minus Foster's enrollment today (447 minus 353). Lincoln and Washington come from the same projections but can't be separated cleanly (Lincoln could be 77 to 125). Orrington 41 is a Census estimate, because the district's Orrington projection doesn't show the Dewey students its own map sends there. Then the dual-language rule applies: all 102 dual-language students go to Lincoln, and the 212 regular students split in the same proportions, about 68 Lincoln, 63 Foster, 53 Washington and 28 Orrington. So Lincoln gets about 170 Dewey students in all. The grade-by-grade numbers apply those shares to each Dewey grade, so they are rough. Receiving schools' regular class counts are also estimates, and other border changes on the same map (such as Washington to Dawes) aren't included. [13] [7] [20]

  • The two buildings' own line items cover about 16 jobs (principals, office, custodians, library, intervention). About 2 are interventionists, who move with the children they serve, so closing would remove about 14 if the cuts actually happen. [1]
  • Fewer buildings may also let the district combine specialist and support roles that every building needs, such as art, music, PE, nursing and lunch staff. Any such cuts would be part of the 56 certified and 40 classified positions, not in addition to them, and so would the 6 to 8 classroom teachers above. The building jobs are different: they are priced in the closure line, not the staffing line. If the 103 also include building jobs already priced in the closure line, the plan counts them twice; the district hasn't said. [9] [1]
Dig in: pricing, other counts, and where else the money could come from

How positions are priced. The plan prices each certified position at $68,000 salary plus $15,000 benefits ($83,000), and this page uses that rate. [1] The state's salary report puts average certified compensation near $121,000 in 2026-27. [14] The two may measure different things: the district's benefit amount is flat per position, and the state figure likely includes pension costs. We don't know whether $68,000 is an average salary, an open-position rate or a new-hire rate.

How the public counts fit together. The October 13 presentation lists 225.8 positions in two groups: 103 under closures and consolidation (6 administrators, 56 certified, 41 classified) and 122.8 under non-mandated programs such as child care and Head Start (2, 32.8 and 88). Together that is 8 administrators, 88.8 certified and 129 classified, which matches the Sun-Times count and the district's "over 200." The October 7 plan's 102 is the first group, with one fewer classified position. [9] [10] [17] [1]

Positions aren't the same as people. A position can be an open job or a retirement that isn't refilled. The district hasn't said how many of these cuts would be layoffs. The plan does set aside $750,000 for unemployment benefits, which suggests some will be. [1] The sustainability page also says no school-based role, job category or program within the school day is fully eliminated, so the cuts are spread across roles rather than whole jobs disappearing. [17]

A fair test for every line. We test the closure claim against the record below. We haven't done the same for the rest of the plan. If the staffing line delivers the way the April 2026 plan did (45 of 55.5 positions, about 81%), its $7.3M of positions would yield about $1.4M less. [5]

The section math. Next year's grades 1–5 are this fall's K–4. For each grade we take the closing school's regular students, split them the way the district's map does, add them to each receiving school's regular students, and count classes before and after. Lincolnwood's students go 269 to Willard and 39 to Walker by the district's count, with its 23 STEP students going to Orrington separately. Dewey's go to Lincoln, Foster, Washington and Orrington; the district hasn't published that split, so we estimate it: by home address about 101, 94, 78 and 41, with Lincoln anywhere from 77 to 125. Applying the dual-language rule, the 212 regular students split about 68, 63, 53 and 28, and Lincoln also takes all 102 dual-language students. [7] [20] All 102 of Dewey's dual-language students go to Lincoln as one strand, about 17 per grade, so those 5 classes carry over unchanged. Class size is a goal, not a cap. The teachers' contract (Article 9(A)) sets goals of 23 in K–2 and 25 in grades 3–5. A class over the goal gets a review with the principal and may get extra support, such as a co-teacher, an aide or reduced duties; it doesn't automatically become two classes. [26] In practice, the district's fall 2026 class list at the five schools without dual-language programs matches "one class per 24 students, rounded up" in 28 of 30 grades. One exception runs over: Orrington's 3rd grade has 52 students in 2 classes, 26 each. [6] [13] So we start from the district's current classes and ask how many fewer the merged grades would need at different sizes. At the contract goals: Dewey 5, Lincolnwood 1, so 6. Letting merged classes run one student over the goal (24 in K–2, 26 in 3–5): 7. Two over (25 and 27), or 26 everywhere: 8. Only at 28 in every grade does it reach 13, with 19 classes above the goal. Dewey's count holds for any Lincoln share from 77 to 125 and any Orrington share from 29 to 53. Running classes over the goal trades a teacher for support: a teacher costs $83,000 at the plan's rate and an aide about $53,000, so a class kept large with a full-time aide saves only about $30,000. [1] Limits: grade-by-grade dual-language counts are estimates (the dashboard reports each strand's total), receiving schools' regular class sizes are estimates at Foster and Washington, and other border moves on the same map (Washington to Dawes, Lincoln to Oakton) also change those schools' classes and aren't included. The district has the student-level projection that would settle this. [13] [6] [10]

This doesn't say which cut is better. It says the closures aren't the only way to find this much money, so the choice should rest on what each option costs students and families.

How much would closing them actually save?

Likely between about $0.1M and $1.8M a year, not $2.9M. The answer turns on two decisions the plan doesn't make: whether the jobs are really cut, and whether the buildings are sold.

  • The $2.9M is one year of each building's staff and operating costs. The district calls it "gross" and gives no net figure. [1]
  • If the jobs are cut (Case A): about $1.8M a year after insurance, part of the upkeep on the empty buildings, and added busing. [1] [8]
  • If staffing goes like last year (Case B): about $0.1M. After Kingsley and Bessie Rhodes closed, the district had two more assistant principals and two more custodians, not fewer. [14] [15] [5]
  • Selling the buildings would add about $0.7M a year in either case. The district says it will keep them and won't sell, lease or repurpose them in the short term. [9] [10]
District's claimed savingCost that continuesNet per yearPossible extra, not counted

"If sold" assumes every building cost stops once the district no longer owns the building. A one-time sale price would help reserves, not the yearly budget, so it isn't included.

Dig in: the math, the evidence and its limits

Why Case B lands near zero. The district credited the Kingsley and Bessie Rhodes closures with $2.02M of staffing savings. [1] In the first year after they closed, assistant principals went from 12 to 14 on the state salary report, [14] and the district's staff file shows custodians up 2. [15] Some roles shrank (interventionists 20 to 19, librarians 15 to 14), [15] but the district hasn't said whether those cuts came from the closures or from falling enrollment. Overall staff fell about 3%, in line with the 3% enrollment drop. [5] LoDN's range for the realized staffing saving runs from a $0.5M net cost to a $0.2M saving; the midpoint, a net cost of about 7% of the staffing lines, is applied here. (Counting building costs too, the realized total is a $0.2M net cost to a $0.7M saving.) [5]

Didn't last year's cuts happen? Mostly, yes: the April 2026 plan cut 55.5 positions and the staff file shows about 45 fewer. But that drop matches the 3% fall in enrollment, the kind of cut that happens with or without closures. The question here is narrower: did closing two buildings remove building jobs on top of that? The record so far says no. [5] [15]

Limits of that evidence. It is one year. Last year's count was headcount and this year's is FTE. And Foster opened this fall with Bessie Rhodes' dual-language program, [5] [18] so some of the added assistant principals and custodians may be Foster's own staff. If so, Case B is too pessimistic and the truth sits closer to Case A.

How each number is calculated

Dewey + Lincolnwood on the district's proposed map. The chart, the table above and this table come from the same calculation.

Where each line comes from

  • District's claim. The October 7 plan, section 6A, line by line: Dewey $1,480,065, Lincolnwood $1,416,954. [1]
  • Case A staffing (assumption). Principals, assistant principals, office staff, custodians and librarians go. Interventionists move with the children they serve, so they aren't counted as saved. LoDN's earlier building-use page estimated a typical closure at $0.47–0.82M a year before busing, using general salary figures before the district published these line items. The line items are specific to Dewey and Lincolnwood and include an assistant principal at each, so Case A uses them; it is the best case if every listed position is cut. [6] [1]
  • Case B staffing (record plus estimate). Applies last year's result, described above. [5] [14] [15]
  • Buildings kept. Insurance ($428,402 of the claim) continues in full on a building the district owns. [1] Repairs, utilities, security and technology ($468,332) partly continue. The district hasn't published what an idle building costs, so the shares are our assumption, set by what the district plans for each building: 75% at Dewey, which has to stay ready to reopen as a swing school, and 25% at Lincolnwood, which is held for a future rebuild. That is about 52% overall, and it's the same in both cases, because what an empty building costs doesn't depend on whether staff are cut. [9] Other districts' mothballed schools cost far less to hold, about $60,000 a building a year in Chicago and $49,000–85,000 in Charleston, which suggests the 25% end fits a building that is truly shut down. [27] [28] Each 25 points on these shares moves the net by about $0.12M a year. Supplies, waste removal, copiers and discretionary spending stop.
  • Added busing. Priced from the district's February 2026 transportation memo at $80K per 55 new riders. Both cases use the same busing, since it depends on the map, not on staffing. [8]
  • Fewer classrooms. A possible extra, priced at the district's $83K rate. [1] The model's count assumes children spread evenly across grades, so it is an upper bound. With real class sizes, the district's map splitting students across receiving schools, and Dewey's dual-language classes moving intact, the two closures together free about 6 classes at the contract's class-size goals, or 7 to 8 if merged classes run 1–2 students over them, about $0.5–0.66M a year, and only if those teaching positions are actually cut. Classes kept over the goal may need aides, which would offset part of that. [13] [20]
  • Not counted. One-time moving, IT and renovation costs. The plan sets aside a separate $1M implementation allowance ($750K unemployment benefits, $250K consulting). [1] Special education impacts are still to come. [10]

What does it cost students and families?

Most of the costs of closing aren't in the $2.9M. Children move, programs move, buildings get fuller, and some trips get longer.

The district's case for consolidation: more consistent class sizes, more enrichment and extracurricular options, larger teams of teachers to collaborate, and more room for specialists. These benefits aren't priced either. [9]

EffectWhat the record shows
Children who change schools713, by the district's count, including 329 who are English learners, low-income or have IEPs. [22] Some had just moved to Lincolnwood after Kingsley closed. [9] [10]
Where they goMost Lincolnwood students to Willard; most Dewey students to Lincoln. [10]
Who can stayDual-language students stay in their program wherever they live, transfer students stay at their school, and current 6th and 7th graders stay at their middle school. Regular K–4 students in areas that shift between schools that stay open get no option to stay. [20]

Building conditionWillard is the most worn neighborhood elementary (condition index 45.4%). Lincoln is about the same as Dewey (31.0% vs 30.5%). [2]
Programs that moveAll of Dewey's dual-language strand, 102 students, moves to Lincoln, which has none today. Lincolnwood's STEP students (23) move to Orrington. After the move, every dual-language strand except Foster's is in south Evanston (Dawes, Oakton, Washington, Lincoln); north Evanston loses its nearby option. By the district's count, about a third of the Spanish-dominant dual-language students in the Nichols feeder area already live in Lincoln's attendance area. [9] [20] [9] [13]
AccessibilityDewey is one of three older neighborhood elementaries with an elevator. Lincoln has one; Willard has one. [2]
Added busingAbout 91 more children become eligible for a bus on the district's map (our count), roughly $45K–160K a year. A map drawn to avoid hazard crossings adds none. The district's own estimate isn't published yet. Not counted: busing Dewey's dual-language students to Lincoln, and transportation for students allowed to stay outside their new area. [7] [8] [10] [20]
One-time movingAfter Kingsley and Bessie Rhodes closed, the district moved 127 teachers, 3,486 boxes and about 2,800 pieces of furniture last summer. It hasn't published what that cost, and it isn't in the closure savings. [25]
Families who may leaveAfter the Kingsley closure was announced, 10% of 117 responding families said they were unlikely to stay in D65 and 5% were unsure. [16] The district hasn't published how many actually left.

"Our count" means LoDN's model, which places children using Census data. It overcounts at some borders: on the district's map it finds 1,094 children moving where the district counts 713. Part of the gap is the district's placement rules: dual-language and transfer students stay put, but our model counts them as movers. Washington is half dual-language (195 of 387) and Oakton about a fifth (75 of 367). Taking those students out brings our Washington-to-Dawes count from 220 to about 109, close to the district's 99, and our total to about 970. [20] Use these counts as rough sizes. The family survey was voluntary, not a random sample. [7] [16]

Dig in: busing next to the transportation budget and the savings
  • Small next to the budget. Up to $160K a year of added busing is a sliver of a $9.5M transportation bill. [4] [8]
  • Not small next to the savings. If staffing goes like last year, the saving before busing is about $0.28M, and busing can take more than half of it.
  • The map decides it. The district's map adds about 91 bus-eligible children (our count); a map drawn around hazard crossings adds none. [7]

  • Spending more than doubled from FY22 to FY24 while enrollment fell. Most of the fund pays outside contractors ($8.6M in FY25) for special education, preschool and program placements. [4]
  • General-education routes: about $2.4M a year for about 1,104 riders, roughly $2,174 per rider, including King Arts. The district's status table lists 796 general-education riders, so cost per rider may be closer to $3,000. [8] The FY27 budget shows general-education busing at $3.1M in FY26 (unaudited) and $3.4M budgeted for FY27, more than the memo's $2.4M; on that basis, cost per rider is about $2,800 to $3,900. [23]
  • Added busing math: ceil(91 ÷ 110) × $45,000 = $45K at the low end; ceil(91 ÷ 55) × $80,000 = $160K at the high end. [8]
  • Why this is lower than LoDN's earlier estimate. Our building-use analysis put a typical closure at about 120 new riders. That came from the district's 2025 closure scenarios, none of which closed Dewey, and whose Lincolnwood scenario sent students to Orrington rather than next-door Willard. The 91 here is counted on the actual FY28 map with the 2026-27 hazard list, so it fits this proposal better. It still places children by Census data, not home addresses, so treat it as an estimate. The earlier page priced its high end at the average cost per rider (about $2,200); added riders are better priced by the routes they add, as here. [6] [3] [7] [8]

What about the buildings?

Dewey is in better shape than most of the district's schools, which fits the district's plan to keep it as a "swing school" while others are renovated. Lincolnwood is mid-pack. Either way, repair money is saved only if a building is sold or retired, and the district proposes keeping both.

  • Why the district picked these two. Dewey: the Nichols feeder schools have lost 33% of their enrollment in a decade, Dewey has a lower share of marginalized students, its campus has limited outdoor space and slightly fewer classrooms and breakout spaces, and the district calls it a "solid physical plant that could be used as a swing school." Lincolnwood: the Haven feeder schools have also lost 33%, the district says they need the most capital spending, most Lincolnwood students fit at Willard, and its site could be renovated or rebuilt. [9] [22] [21]
  • The condition data backs up the district on Dewey. It has the third-best condition index of the nine neighborhood elementaries (30.5%) and an elevator. The facility plan dates the building to 1940, with additions in 2009 and 2011; the district dates it to 1906. Lincolnwood sits in the middle (37.2%). Together they need $23.5M of work from 2027 to 2033. [2] [22]
  • The Haven capital claim depends on the measure. From 2027 to 2033, Lincolnwood, Orrington and Willard need $35.1M together, less than Chute's three elementaries ($37.9M) or Nichols' ($41.2M). Per student they need slightly more ($41K vs. $39–40K), because the schools are smaller. Within Haven, Willard needs more than Lincolnwood soon ($15.0M vs. $12.5M, and the worst condition of the nine); Lincolnwood needs more over 2027–2080 ($31.6M vs. $25.7M). The district hasn't said which measure it used. [2] [22]
  • The $58M maintenance saving assumes the buildings are retired. The district says the closures save $58M in future maintenance over 20 years. It used the same kind of figure, $57M, for Kingsley and Bessie Rhodes. That matches the facility plan's total for the two buildings from 2027 to 2080, with costs rising 4.5% a year: $26.7M + $31.6M = $58.3M. That span is 54 years, not 20, and the money is saved only if the buildings go. The district plans to keep both. [9] [2]
  • Willard takes most Lincolnwood children. Lincoln, which takes most Dewey children, is about the same as Dewey (31.0%). [2] [10]
  • The next two summers' repairs go mostly to middle schools. The district's plan for 2027 and 2028 is $17.3M of work, aimed at life-safety fixes at Haven, Chute and Nichols. Elementary schools share $350K a year for their most urgent items and $750K a year for boilers and other equipment, plus a Walker roof pending approval. No project is listed for Willard, Lincoln or Washington, the schools taking most Dewey and Lincolnwood students. [25]
  • How it's paid for. The plan calls for about $9–10M of life-safety bonds and $8.3–8.5M of district money over the two summers. The FY27 budget books $22M of life-safety bond proceeds and moves $2.4M a year into capital; the district hasn't reconciled the two. Its own capital target is $2.7M a year, against a recommended $20M. [25] [23] [24]
  • Keeping a building keeps its bills. A swing school has to stay ready to open, so most of Dewey's $11.0M of work is likely still needed. The district plans a November 2028 referendum to build or fully renovate two schools. [22] [2]
  • Enrollment is falling, which is a fair long-run reason to have fewer buildings. K-5 enrollment fell from 4,991 in 2015-16 to about 3,500 this fall, and smaller grades are moving up. [13]

Four paths for Dewey + Lincolnwood, in today's dollars. The yearly operating budget and the building repair bill are separate pots of money, so they're shown side by side, not added. Yearly savings are the net figures from the section above; repairs avoided are the $23.5M in the 2026 Facility Master Plan. [1] [2]

This year's kindergarten (534) and grades 1–2 (about 555 each) are smaller than grades 3–5 (about 624), so K-5 keeps shrinking as they move up. [13] Building costs use the district's average line items for Dewey and Lincolnwood ($1.45M a year, gross). [1] Research generally puts efficient elementary size at 300–500 students. [12] This is the strongest long-run case for fewer buildings. It doesn't change this year's savings: teaching jobs follow enrollment with or without closures, while principals, office staff and custodians follow buildings.

Is there an option the plan leaves out?

Yes. King Arts, the district-wide K-8 magnet, has the best-condition building, about 200 open seats and the most bus riders, and the plan doesn't price any option for it.

  • King Arts has 443 students in a building with 651 seats. [18] [13]
  • Its condition index is 17.2%, the best of any school assessed. [2]
  • 286 of its students ride general-education buses, between a quarter and a third of all such riders in the district (796 to 1,104, depending on the count), roughly $0.6M a year. [8]
  • A November 2025 scenario would have made King Arts a K-5 neighborhood school. It was dropped. The October plan prices no King Arts option, so it can't be weighed against closing two neighborhood schools. [3] [1]
  • The district's presentation gives its reasons for keeping King Arts: it preserves a K–8 magnet alternative, hosts RISE, serves students from across the district, and gives a chance to rethink its program. It doesn't put a cost on keeping it. [9]
Dig in: caveats
  • Not all of the $0.6M would be saved: about 130 King Arts riders qualify through hazard routes and would likely still ride to a neighborhood school. [8]
  • The busing estimate multiplies 286 riders by the average cost per rider. Magnet routes run longer, and the rider count behind the average is uncertain (796 vs about 1,104). [8]
  • King Arts houses RISE, a special education program. Any change has to say where RISE goes and what that costs. [3]
  • The magnet has its own value to families. The point is only that its costs aren't on the table.

Why is there a deficit?

Spending didn't come down when enrollment fell, and federal pandemic relief wound down.

  • K-8 enrollment fell 22%, from 7,371 in 2015-16 to 5,748 in 2024-25. [13]
  • Operating spending rose from $112M to $167M over the same years. After inflation, spending per student rose 42%. [4]
  • The district points to pay and staffing. The FY27 budget adds $9.0M of salaries and benefits in one year (salaries +4.6%, benefits +19.2%), and health costs are trending up 12% a year. By the district's figures it has one licensed staff member for every 8.5 students against 10.6 at peer districts, and one other staff member per 10.6 students against 23.5. [24]
  • Federal aid, swelled by pandemic relief, peaked at about $16M a year in FY22–FY23 and fell to $10.8M in FY25. [4]
  • Illinois' tax cap limits yearly property tax growth to the lower of inflation or 5%, so the district's main revenue source slows when inflation cools. [19]
  • This year's gap is smaller than $20M. The adopted FY27 budget shows $185.0M of operating spending against $179.9M of revenue, a $5.1M gap, or $1.5M before one-time transfers for Foster. Reserves are falling: 100 days of spending at the end of FY25, 92 in FY26, and a projected 78 in FY27, below the board's 90-day goal. [23]
  • Cash is tight enough to borrow short-term. The September 14 board agenda included a resolution authorizing up to $15.96M of tax anticipation warrants, short-term borrowing repaid from property taxes not yet collected. The same presentation lists avoiding short-term borrowing among the community's priorities. [24]

Audited results FY15–FY25, then the district's November 2025 projection (dashed). The dotted line is revenue continuing at its FY19–FY25 pace. [4] [3]

Dig in: how growth assumptions change the gap

FY30 gap between spending and revenue, starting from the FY26 budget, under different yearly growth rates. The district's November 2025 projection sits in the top-left cell. [3] [4]

Each extra point of yearly revenue growth closes about $8M of the FY30 gap. The district's November 2025 projection assumed revenue grows about 2.5% a year and spending about 4.0%; its September 2026 presentation uses 2.9% and 5.8%, a wider spread than either column here. [24] From FY19 to FY25, revenue other than federal aid grew 3.9% and spending 4.6%. The lower revenue rate widens the gap by about $11M; the lower spending rate narrows it by about $5M. [3] [4] Growth rates start at FY19 because FY18's revenue jump of about $27M appears to be a one-time shift in property tax timing. Measured from FY16, revenue and spending grew about equally; from FY19, spending grew faster. [4]

Will the plan keep the budget balanced?

The plan shows one year of cuts. It doesn't show how the gap stays closed while the costs that opened it keep growing.

  • Three numbers, three meanings. $20M is the district's savings goal, tied to balanced budgets and rebuilding cash reserves to 90 days; it hasn't shown how the figure was derived. Without action, the district now projects a yearly shortfall of $3.9M in FY28 growing to $21.6M in FY30; its November 2025 projection had $12M by FY30. [24] [3] $14.9M is what the plan nets after its own new spending, and the presentation shows the two numbers side by side without reconciling them. [9] The goal is far larger than the FY28 shortfall and close to FY30's, which may mean it is sized for the next three years and for rebuilding reserves; the district hasn't said.
  • The October 7 plan reports gross figures only: $21.4M. [1] The district's October 13 presentation sets aside money for capital and teaching investments and one-time costs, leaving about $14.9M net. [9]
  • The district hasn't shown how the $20M goal was derived or whether it is gross or net. The presentation says the plan is meant to rebuild cash reserves to 90 days, without saying how much of the $20M that takes. [1] [10] [9]
  • From FY19 to FY25, employee benefits and special education programs each grew 57%, while operating revenue grew 24%. [4]
  • The shortfall the district projects without action. Its September 14 presentation labels the years: a $3.9M shortfall in FY28, $15.3M in FY29, $21.6M in FY30, $28.5M in FY31 and $36.0M in FY32, with cash falling from 77 days of spending to −99. The $20M target is set for FY28, but it is about the size of the FY30 shortfall; FY28's is $3.9M. The district hasn't said how it chose $20M. [24] [23]

The FY27 budget already moves $2.4M a year into capital projects. The district hasn't said whether the plan's $4.7M for capital is on top of it. [23] [22]

An illustration, not a forecast. If spending after the cuts grew 4.6% a year (its FY19–25 pace) and revenue grew the 2.5% the district projects, the gap would reopen by about $3.5M a year, using up a $14.9M reset in about four years. At revenue's FY19–25 pace (3.9%), it would reopen by about $1.2M a year. This is our arithmetic on a $165M budget, ignoring compounding. [3] [4]

The plan's "limit future costs" section lists budget discipline and controlling expense growth, with no dollar amounts. [9]

Can we rely on the district's estimates?

The estimates aren't invented, but they have changed without explanation, and savings have been counted before they happened.

  • Kingsley's closure was priced at $2.00M a year in October 2025 and $1.66M three weeks later, with different lines included. [3]
  • Lincolnwood's closure was priced at $2.15M a year in October 2025 and $1.42M in October 2026, using a different method. [3] [1]
  • The plan counts $3.0M a year from last year's closures as "already reflected in projections." [1] LoDN's review finds the realized total, staffing and building costs together, between a $0.2M net cost and a $0.7M saving. [5] If savings were counted that didn't happen, the real gap is larger than shown.
  • Spending ran $14.1M over budget in FY23 and $7.7M over in FY24, then $13.3M under in FY25. [4]

Questions the numbers leave open

Each of these changes how much the closures would actually save.

What's next: administrators asked the board to advance the plan on November 9, with three public hearings for each school in December. [22]

  1. How was the $20M target set? The presentation links it to balanced budgets and 90 days of cash, but the plan nets $14.9M. Is $20M before or after new spending, and how much rebuilds reserves? [9] [1] [10]
  2. Which of the 103 "closures and consolidation" positions come from closing Dewey and Lincolnwood? Split them by role between the closures and other consolidation (who fills them follows seniority rules), and say whether any duplicate the $1.82M of staff already in the closure line. What does the $68,000 salary represent? [9] [1]
  3. What did Kingsley and Bessie Rhodes actually save? The district counts $3.0M a year. The staff records available so far show close to nothing. [1] [5]
  4. What does an idle building cost? The district says it will keep both buildings and won't sell, lease or repurpose them in the short term. What will they cost each year while they wait? How was the $58M maintenance saving calculated, when both buildings are kept? [9]
  5. What will busing and the receiving schools cost? The district's transportation estimate isn't published. Willard needs $15.0M of work, and the 2027–28 repair plan lists nothing for Willard, Lincoln or Washington. Is the life-safety borrowing $22M, as the budget shows, or $9–10M, as the repair plan says? [10] [2] [25] [23]
  6. Why isn't King Arts priced? It has about 200 open seats and the most bus riders. [13] [8]
What these numbers leave out, and how they were built
  • Programs. The model moves children, not programs such as dual-language, STEP or RISE. The district's rules keep dual-language and transfer students in place and move Dewey's strand to Lincoln and Lincolnwood's STEP to Orrington; the text above adjusts for this, but the explorer's counts don't. [20]
  • Values. The model would close Foster, which opened this fall; we excluded it by hand. That's a values call, made in the open.
  • Learning. Nothing here measures outcomes, culture or the cost of disruption to a child.
  • Middle schools. Feeder patterns into Chute, Haven and Nichols aren't modeled.
  • Who actually enrolls. Children are placed where Census counts say they live. In the district's new Dawes zone the model finds 551 children where the district projects 395, so treat "our count" figures as rough. [7]
  • One-time costs. Moving, packing, IT and renovation aren't counted. They come first and make every closure look worse in year one.

Inputs. October 1, 2026 enrollment for the ten neighborhood elementaries (3,204 K-5 children). [18] Children placed on 200-foot cells using ACS 2020-24 and 2020 Census data. Capacities from the district's October 7 FY28 table, or a conservative table. Hazard routes from the district's 2026-27 list. [7]

Optimization. For each set of open schools, a linear program assigns children to schools, minimizing walking distance plus penalties for bus-eligible and moved children, with each school capped at 95% of capacity.

Money. Closure savings start from the district's line items and remove what the evidence says won't be saved. [1] Busing is priced from the February 2026 memo. [8] Classrooms are priced at the district's $83K rate. [1] Deficit history uses each Annual Financial Report's operating funds, with CPI-U for inflation. [4]

Limits. Distances are straight-grid, not walking routes. The explorer's class counts for other school combinations assume children are spread evenly across grades, so they run high; the Dewey and Lincolnwood class analysis above uses real grade sizes.

Code and data: LoDN repo, dataanalysis/. The class-merge counts are reproduced by build_fy28_class_merge.py. The boundary model behind the explorer is not yet in the repo.
